action_criteria.expected_evidence: Gait that improves with a dual task and is inconsistent with normal strength, reflexes, coordination and sensation, with walking-on-ice and knee-buckling patterns
action_criteria.label: Examine the gait and the limbs for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: Three weeks of slow, effortful walking with knee buckling: the diagnosis rests on positive signs, here the improvement of gait with a dual task and the inconsistency between a normal limb examination and the gait, and on the absence of pyramidal, cerebellar or sensory signs, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B; Daum 2014).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Walk times that vary widely between trials and improve under a dual task
action_criteria.label: Timed gait and balance assessment, single and dual task
action_criteria.rationale: Repeated timed walks, alone and under a dual task, measure the variability and the dual-task improvement the bedside examination sees and give a baseline for gait retraining (Nielsen 2015).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cord compression or intramedullary lesion
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI without contrast, once, if a cord question remains
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical myelopathy can present as a gait disorder, but normal reflexes, no Hoffmann sign or clonus, normal sensation without a level and normal sphincters make it unlikely; one non-contrast spine MRI is acceptable but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cerebellar, brainstem or hemispheric lesion
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast, once, if a structural question remains
action_criteria.rationale: There is no cerebellar, pyramidal or cranial nerve sign; one non-contrast brain MRI is acceptable to look for a structural cause of the gait disorder but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies anxiety and mood to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify her returning anxiety to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional gait disorder) based on the improvement of gait with a dual task and the inconsistency between a normal examination of strength, tone, reflexes, coordination and sensation and the severely impaired gait, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus), with gait retraining.
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid generalized anxiety disorder.

avoided_actions.rationale: She has had no loss of consciousness, syncope or palpitations, and the knee buckling occurs in full awareness; an ECG answers no question.
There is no murmur, syncope or embolic question; an echocardiogram answers nothing in this patient.
The knee buckling occurs in full awareness with no light-headedness or palpitations; nothing suggests an arrhythmia.
There is no head injury and no focal or cerebellar sign; a head CT adds radiation and no information.
She is afebrile with no inflammatory, encephalopathic or neuropathic feature and normal reflexes; a lumbar puncture would add risk and change nothing.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in a functional gait disorder and answers no question in this patient.
Strength is 5/5 without wasting or fasciculation, and reflexes and sensation are normal; nerve conduction studies and EMG have no question to answer.
Vibration and joint position sense are normal with no sensory level; somatosensory evoked potentials answer no question here.
There is no bradykinesia, rigidity or tremor, and the slow gait improves with a dual task; there is no parkinsonism for a dopamine transporter scan to confirm or exclude.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — functional gait disorder

differential.key_features: A gait disorder in a young adult, but no neck pain, normal reflexes without Hoffmann sign or clonus, flexor plantars, normal sensation without a level, normal hand function and normal sphincters.
Wide-based unsteady gait, but normal finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin and eye movements, no truncal sway when sitting, and a gait that improves when she is distracted.
Unsteadiness on standing, but no leg shaking or relief on walking or sitting, and the difficulty is in walking rather than standing still.
Knee giving way can reflect proximal weakness, but strength is 5/5 in all muscle groups with normal bulk and no give-way on testing.

key_clinical_evidence: Her gait improves with a dual task, and it is inconsistent with full strength and normal tone, reflexes, coordination and sensation: positive signs of a functional gait disorder.

Walking on ice, sudden knee buckling with recovery before a fall, excessive slowness and a Romberg sway that lessens with distraction are described features of functional gait disorder (Daum 2014) and support it.

Normal reflexes without Hoffmann sign or clonus, no sensory level and normal sphincters make cervical myelopathy unlikely, and normal coordination without truncal ataxia makes a cerebellar cause unlikely; imaging is optional.
The new job and the return of her anxiety are supportive context and a treatment target; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Severe disability is common in functional gait disorder and does not indicate structural disease; the positive signs and the normal limb examination decide.
red_herrings.data_point: She holds on to furniture, cannot manage the stairs and has stopped working
red_herrings.intended_effect: Infer a severe structural deficit and order brain and whole-spine imaging, nerve studies and a lumbar puncture

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive signs of the examination.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset a week after starting a demanding new job
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the stressor alone, without positive signs

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND; it is a treatment target, and the diagnosis rests on the examination.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder, treated 2 years ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an anxiety explanation without examining for positive signs; or dismiss the gait disorder as 'just anxiety'

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward case: three weeks of slow, effortful walking with knee buckling after starting a new job, with dual-task improvement and a normal limb examination.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: The required work-up is the examination, which finds a gait that improves with a dual task and is inconsistent with a normal limb examination; a timed gait assessment is recommended. The severe disability invites spinal and brain imaging, nerve studies and a lumbar puncture, and the new job invites a diagnosis from the stressor alone.
key_positive_signs: gait improvement with a dual task

patient.history_present_illness: A 28-year-old right-handed woman is admitted from the emergency department with 3 weeks of difficulty walking. It developed over two days, a week after she started a new job as a customer service team leader at a call center, a post she had wanted but finds very demanding. She now walks slowly and with great effort, holding on to furniture at home, and several times a day one knee suddenly gives way; she has always caught herself before falling and has not been injured. Walking is worse when she is tired or in a crowded place. She stopped working 2 weeks ago, her partner now drives her everywhere, and she came to the emergency department because she could no longer manage the stairs to their apartment. She reports no weakness or numbness of the legs, no neck or back pain, no bladder or bowel symptoms, no clumsiness of the hands, no double vision, slurred speech or vertigo, and no shaking of the legs when standing. She has had no recent illness, vaccination, new medicine, alcohol excess or weight loss. Her anxiety, treated with cognitive behavioral therapy 2 years ago, has returned since she started the job.

neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin accurate bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements normal. Sits unsupported without truncal sway.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Eye movements full with normal pursuit and saccades, no nystagmus. Facial strength and sensation normal. Palate, tongue and jaw jerk normal.
neurological_exam.gait: Walks very slowly with short, shuffling steps on a slightly wide base, knees and hips held stiff, arms held out from the body and the feet barely leaving the floor, as if walking on ice. Twice during a 10 m walk a knee suddenly buckles and she recovers before falling. While subtracting serial 7s from 100 she walks noticeably faster with a near-normal stride. Romberg: large sway with the eyes closed from the first second, which lessens when she is asked to identify numbers traced on her forearm. Tandem gait not attempted because of fear of falling.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented, anxious about falling, cooperative. Speech fluent and normally articulated. Attention and memory intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal in all limbs, with no spasticity or catch. Strength 5/5 in all muscle groups of the arms and legs, with no give-way. Finger taps, hand opening and foot taps are fast and full with no decrement. Hoover sign negative bilaterally. No tremor, no fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in the arms and legs. No Hoffmann sign and no clonus. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration and joint position sense normal in all four limbs. No sensory level on the trunk.

physical_exam.spine: No spinal tenderness or deformity; neck movements full and painless.
